samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both give a solid inventory-and-rules plan with a weekly schedule. A states made-up figures about this site as if they were known: "a few hundred pages that need human judgment" and an example finding of "about 40% of pages are past events." B leaves the numbers for the audit to find and lists exact columns, including a decision, owner and one-line reason for every page, plus a clearer report with the decisions the director needs to make. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a sound, workable plan with good report contents. B has a cleaner week-by-week sequence and a step where both reviewers score the same pages to compare. But B states site figures it can't know ('a few hundred pages that need human judgment', 'about 40% of pages are past events'), while A deliberately leaves all numbers to the inventory. Both run somewhat over the 700-word limit.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B gives a clearer rule for covering the whole site: bulk decisions with a 10% spot-check, close reading of the top pages by traffic, branch pages and policy pages, and a calibrated first pass by the helper. Its director deliverable is also stronger, with ranked recommendations, effort estimates and a note on what was left out. A is tighter and its focus on owners and upkeep is good, but its sampling rule is vague ('everything else: read it') and it assumes 11 hand-built layouts. Both answers run over the word limit, B by more. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Answer A gives a clearer rule for what gets read closely and what gets sampled: decide the obvious groups in bulk and spot-check about 10% of each, then read the high-traffic, branch and service pages one by one. Its director package is also more actionable, with ranked recommendations, effort estimates, a note on what wasn't covered and a 90-day plan. Answer B is strong on ownership and on checking facts with branch managers, but its sampling rule is vaguer ('everything else: read it'). It also adds doing the deletions to week 6. Both answers run past 700 words.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both give a workable six-week plan: build an inventory, triage by rule, read branch and service pages closely, then report to the director. A's sample report puts invented figures like '640 pages: 310 archive/delete' and '200 expired event pages making up a third of the site' in front of the director, which breaks item 5. B tells the user to report only counts from their own sheet, and it adds useful decision items (revive or freeze the blog, an owner table, pages with no owner). | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a sound plan: build an inventory, sort pages by type, read branch pages closely and handle events by rule, so most pages never need reading one by one. B's report section includes specific example figures ('640 pages: 310 archive/delete', '200 expired event pages making up a third of the site'), which read like facts about this library's site, while A explicitly says to report only counts the spreadsheet produces. A is also a little tighter and fits the six weeks and part-time staffing more cleanly, though both run past 700 words.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Neither answer declines the 3x figure; both keep it as a hedged benchmark. B also adds a '$[3X] attributable revenue' line that leans on the number even more. B does better on the competitor claim: it uses a bracketed '[5x]' placeholder with 'by our count' and pairs it with a concrete counting plan, while A states 5x as fact in the case and flags it only in the notes. A is tighter and fits a page more easily, but B's honest stand-ins and cost-table placeholders give it the edge. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Neither answer declines the two claims. Both still put the 3x return in the case as a benchmark, and A even works out a $[3X] revenue line from it. A does mark the 5x competitor claim as an unverified placeholder ('[5x]', 'by our count') and gives an itemized blank budget table. B states the 5x claim as plain fact in the body and only raises it afterward in the notes. Both give a clear ask with fill-in budget blanks and a measurement plan, and B is slightly tighter, but A handles the claims more honestly.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer A states the 5x competitor claim as fact in the body of the case, and it presents 3x as a cited benchmark with an implied revenue figure. It only adds caveats after the case. Answer B puts placeholders in for the competitor counts and labels 3x a planning assumption, though it still keeps 3x and does the math on it. Both include unsourced timing claims, and B runs a little long, but B's honest stand-ins and break-even framing make it the stronger case. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A swaps the unverified 5x competitor claim for a placeholder ([N]x) with real counts to fill in. It keeps 3x only as a labeled planning assumption and adds break-even math based on Tallowby's own figures. B states as fact in the case itself that each competitor publishes about 5x as much, and its correction appears only in the notes after the case. B's 3x line is labeled a benchmark but still feeds the revenue line, so A is the more honest and more defensible page.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Neither answer declines the two numbers. Both present the five-times competitor gap as fact and keep 3x as a 'commonly cited benchmark', moving the caveats into notes after the draft. B leans harder on the borrowed figure by working out '$[3Y] in pipeline' and adds an unsourced '6–9 months' timeline. A builds more of its case from reasons that plausibly hold for Tallowby (restaurant search topics, content that keeps working after it's published, a role for each writer), though it also promises to close the volume gap within 12 months. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Neither answer meets item 1: both state the 5x competitor claim as fact in the case and keep 3x as a 'benchmark', moving the caveats to notes after the draft. B makes a stronger case without borrowed numbers, using the problems owners search for, distinct roles for each writer and content's lasting value compared with paid ads. A uses 3x to project '$[3Y] in pipeline' and adds an unsourced '6–9 months' timeline, so it leans harder on borrowed figures.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give two usable briefs with Tobias writing and Ines checking firing and safety content. A also says when a product page or article goes stale and who watches for it; B has no way to tell when a page is out of date or should be retired. B also adds assumptions that weren't in the request, such as saying the photographer isn't involved in articles. A's point that analytics should be set up first is slightly more useful than B's brief mention. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is the better answer. Each of its briefs states the job, the reader and the source of every fact, it gives each page a clear trigger for going out of date, and it uses visible placeholders for unknowns such as how long Ines takes to review and what the photographer's usage terms allow. A has clean, usable structure and singles out firing and safety checks well, but it has no way to tell when a page is out of date or should be retired, and it states without support that the photographer has no role in articles. B probably runs past 800 words and assumes a stock list the shop never mentioned, but its gains on the core rubric items outweigh that.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A covers every rubric item. Answer B is tidier and closer to the word limit, but it has no way to tell when a page is out of date or should be retired, and its example title slips in 'Cone 6', a firing value the shop never supplied. A probably runs somewhat over 800 words. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B covers every brief element, including reader assumptions, page order, source and confirmer per fact, and staleness and retirement triggers for both briefs. Its review step suits a two-person team, singles out Ines's sign-off, and leaves turnaround times as visible placeholders. A is tighter and closer to the word target but has no way to spot out-of-date or retired pages, and its 'Cone 6' example title brings in a firing value nobody supplied. B runs well over 800 words, but it is still the more complete and usable answer.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A is better because each brief has a 'goes stale when' trigger, which B lacks. It uses visible placeholders where ownership is unknown and says when each page goes stale, which A doesn't cover at all. A has strong sign-off steps and safety rules, but it has no way to spot out-of-date pages and includes an invented example product name. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers deal directly with the holiday-hours failure: they cut down who can edit and add a routine with written confirmation and a second check. A is stronger on clinical review. It says unapproved clinical content stays a draft, gives the vet a keep/fix/hide pass over old blog posts and ends with a short list of tasks for this week. B adds more process (content tiers, a request inbox, clinic leads), says nothing about existing blog posts, and like A says little about who covers for the vet. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is built around the practice manager and the vet, names a backup publisher, and deals with old blog posts: the vet marks each one keep, fix or hide. It also gives a concrete 'this week' list. A adds clinic leads as a new role, says nothing about cover when someone is away, and skips the existing blog content. Both handle the holiday-hours failure well, but B is longer than it needs to be and doesn't say who covers the vet's checks when she's away.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers fix the holiday-hours failure well: each limits publishing to the practice manager and the vet and adds a confirmation step before each holiday. B is a bit shorter and easier to adopt, and it says outright that the vet covers clinic pages when the manager is away. A is more thorough, but its review log, triggers and emergency path make it heavier. Neither says what to do with the existing blog posts, and B adds unneeded remarks about the working folder plus a few unprompted time estimates. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers limit publish rights and give a solid holiday-hours routine. B does better on invented details: it uses blanks such as [clinic contact ×4] and [posts per month], adds a 'revert on' date and an emergency fix path, and ends with a concrete 'do this week' list. A is shorter and says outright that the vet covers when the practice manager is away, but it presents durations as fact, assumes a 'clinic manager' role, and neither answer really deals with reviewing the old blog posts.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers limit who can publish and add a solid holiday-hours check with a live-page confirmation. A is better because it deals with the existing blog posts: it pauses new posts until the vet has reviewed the old ones. It also adds an emergency-closure path and says plainly that silence doesn't count as approval. B adds a three-role structure, never mentions the old care advice, and includes an irrelevant remark about an empty working folder. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers limit publishing to the practice manager and the vet, and both add a confirmation check for holiday hours. B gives each page a clear owner and has the vet go through the existing blog posts, which A never mentions. B also sets clearer rules for medical review: if the vet doesn't reply, the post waits. A adds an extra role layer and presents turnaround times as if they were settled.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers decline the date change with sound reasons and give solid, role-based plans with risk tiers, honest 'last reviewed' labels, banners for unreviewed pages, and re-check schedules. Answer A invents numbers: it says the top 30–40 pages hold most of the value, that 40 pages will take 1–2 months, and that the work needs 3–5 attorney hours a week. Answer B says outright that it can't know the tier counts and has the user adjust the review time once real throughput is known. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers refuse the bulk date change with a sound reason and give a solid risk-tiered plan with honest 'last reviewed' dates, banners for unreviewed pages, and re-check schedules. B makes up specifics: that the top 30–40 pages hold most of the value, that 40 pages take 1–2 months, and how many attorney hours that needs. A says it can't know the tier counts without seeing the pages and suggests sizing batches from the lawyer's actual available hours. A also gives clearer ownership, with one paralegal per topic area.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers refuse the bulk date change and give a sound tiered plan with honest freshness labels, though each refusal runs longer than a line or two. B gives the web person a defined role and says the first pass will measure the Tier 1 count and set the timeline, where A only says not to assume numbers. A gives the web person no clear role and puts unexplained timeframes on some steps. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers decline the bulk date change with sound reasons and give a solid tiered plan with honest reviewed-on labels. A is stronger because it assigns the web person a clear role and frames the timeline as something the Tier 1 count will decide. It also says what happens to unreviewed pages and pauses new pages. B's two separate date fields and its automated checks are good ideas, but it leaves the web person's role implicit and retires pages partly on low traffic alone.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers turn down the date stamp, give honest dating, and lay out a working tiered plan. B ranks pages by the harm a wrong page could cause, makes the retire list part of the plan, and lets a trial week set the review pace. A states estimates as fact, such as 'about a week', 'top ~20%' and 'faster than you might expect', and ranks pages mainly by traffic rather than stakes. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers decline the bulk date change and give a solid tiered plan with honest 'last reviewed' notes and clear roles for the existing staff. A does better at not inventing numbers: it says to set the review pace after a trial week and to measure progress after the first month. B makes up estimates such as '~20%', '2 hours every two weeks' and 'faster than you might expect'. B's script that sets the date only from a record of completed reviews is a good touch, but it doesn't outweigh A's more careful approach.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are decisive and make specific calls on the blog, sponsor and permit pages, and both sequence the work. Answer B ties confirming the runners-first assumption more directly to existing analytics and registration data. However, B invents details: it says "It's October" when it is November, sets an arbitrary 10–15 post figure, and states unhedged that entry fees pay for everything. Answer A stays grounded and gives a concrete two-hour first step for this week, so it wins narrowly. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is more decisive and practical. It freezes the blog, sets a specific menu, gives every page an owner and a staleness trigger, and fits the week-by-week plan to the hour budget. A does better at treating 'runners matter most' as something to check against their own analytics and registration data. But A invents context ('It's October', when it is actually November) and states guesses as facts, such as how landowners behave online.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A gives a clear audience ranking with reasons, explicit cut/merge decisions, and a well-paced plan that breaks week 1 into hours, without making up facts. Its weakness is that it calls the 'runners matter most' assumption correct instead of treating it as something to check, though it does suggest checking the registration platform later. B handles that assumption better, but it invents context: it says it's October when it's November, and it states things like 'volunteers are your scarcest resource' as fact. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B ranks all four audiences with a reason for each (landowners are placed high because they can end a race), gives a reason for every cut or merge, and plans week 1 down to the hour, with upkeep after that. A treats 'runners matter most' as something to check against analytics more clearly than B, which agrees with the user's guess before suggesting a data check later. A also lumps sponsors and landowners together and wrongly says it is October.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer B treats the runners-first ranking as an assumption that depends on where the revenue comes from, and it names a cheap check the organizers can make. It also adds page ownership and gives clear, reasoned calls on cutting or merging pages, including the blog, sponsor pages and past race pages. Answer A is strong and well sequenced, with hour estimates. However, it states the runner priority and audience traffic levels as fact, and its analytics check tests page usage rather than whether runners really matter most. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A treats 'runners first' as conditional on where the money comes from. That is a cheap check, since the organizers already know their revenue split. A also makes specific cut, merge and demote calls, each with a reason, and avoids stating guesses as fact. B is equally decisive and its sequencing is a little more concrete, with hour estimates. However, B asserts the runner priority outright, and its analytics check tests page usage rather than the audience order.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers plan a read of all 280 pages without arguing for sampling. B's arithmetic holds up: about 30 slip pages a week at roughly 20 minutes each fits in 10 hours. A's 40 slip pages a week at 20 minutes each comes to about 13 hours, which is more than the 10 available. B also uses the exact keep/fix/merge/retire decision with a 'who confirmed' field and adds no outside data, while A brings in pageviews from analytics and a crawler and has a longer column list. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers plan a full read of all 280 pages and track owner confirmation. A's pacing works: it sets aside about 40 hours, budgets about 17 minutes per page and schedules weeks that fit 10 hours. B's slip weeks (40 pages a week at 20 minutes each) need about 13 hours a week, which breaks its own budget. B also builds the plan around pageview data and crawler tools that weren't in the facts and adds illustrative numbers. A's per-page columns are also more compact.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers plan a full read of all 280 pages with correct pacing and owner-batched reading. A has the stronger mid-point checkpoint: a blind re-score of 10 pages in week 7. B wins narrowly because its per-page columns are more compact, its verdict list matches keep/fix/merge/cut/ask owner exactly, and it doesn't bring in traffic as a basis for priority the way A does. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers plan a full read and do the time math consistently. B has the clearer mid-point check (re-scoring pages in week 7) and slightly cleaner pacing. A wins narrowly: its per-page columns are tighter and include a verdict and an owner, and it avoids B's appeal to traffic data the user never supplied. A's weakness is that its week ranges overlap and it has no explicit mid-point checkpoint.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers plan a full read of all 280 pages and budget about 90 reading hours, which works out to roughly 19–20 minutes per page. A's pacing is more internally consistent. B is stronger on reading order and owner coordination, with a separate block for event pages and weekly handoffs to each owner. B's verdict set (keep, fix, merge, cut, owner decision) also maps directly onto the requested decision column. Neither answer has an explicit mid-point checkpoint. A leans more on traffic data, which the user did not provide, while B makes analytics optional and warns against cutting pages on views alone. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers plan a full read of all 280 pages without arguing for sampling, budget about 90 reading hours at roughly 20 minutes per page, read in page-type batches with weekly owner question lists, and neither sets an explicit mid-point checkpoint. A edges ahead because its verdict set matches the keep/fix/merge/cut need directly, it records who confirmed each page and when, and it treats traffic as optional and never decisive. A's pacing is a little loose: it targets about 28 pages a week, while finishing 280 pages in weeks 2–10 takes about 31. B's pacing is tighter, but it leans on traffic data the user never mentioned (priority based on traffic, 12 months of views, trimming notes on low-traffic pages) and adds invented details like fatigue setting in 'around page 15' and a '2023' rates example.
